text: Voyager 1 is about to be one light-day from you. How long would you need to reach the nearest star... before you die?

Today we race five ways to get there. On foot. By car. By jet. With the fastest machine humans have ever built. And at the speed of light. Somewhere along the way, a human life runs out. Let's find exactly where.
The nearest star is called Proxima Centauri. It is four point two four light-years away. That sounds close. It is forty trillion kilometers.

Light reaches the Moon in just over one second. It reaches the Sun in eight minutes and twenty seconds. Voyager 1 left Earth in nineteen seventy-seven. It is the farthest object humans have ever made. And it needed almost half a century to get one light-day away.
Proxima Centauri is one thousand five hundred and forty-nine light-days away. Keep that number in mind. Now let's start moving.

One light-year is the distance light travels in a year: about nine point four six trillion kilometers. One light-day is already twenty-six billion kilometers. When engineers send Voyager a command today, the signal needs a full day to arrive, and the answer needs another day to come back. Two days, for a single yes or no.

Let's shrink everything. Imagine the Sun as a ball one meter wide, standing in a park. Earth would be a marble just nine millimeters across, one hundred and seven meters away. You could walk there in a minute. Now, where would Proxima Centauri be? Not in the park. Not in the city. Not even in the same country. On this scale, the nearest star would be about twenty-nine thousand kilometers away. Almost three quarters of the way around the Earth. And between the two balls: nothing. Almost perfectly empty space.
First, we walk. Five kilometers an hour. No breaks, no sleep, a perfectly straight line. At that pace you would reach the Moon in about nine years.

Proxima Centauri? Nine hundred and seventeen million years. For scale: complex animal life exploded on Earth about five hundred and thirty-eight million years ago. You would have had to start walking long before the first animal ever opened its eyes.
So let's take the car. One hundred kilometers an hour, forever. The Moon is now a road trip of one hundred and sixty days.

The nearest star: forty-six million years. The last of the dinosaurs died sixty-six million years ago. If one of them had started driving that very day, it would still have twenty million years to go.

A passenger jet flies at about nine hundred kilometers an hour. That brings the trip down to five point one million years. Our entire genus, Homo, has existed for about two point eight million years. All of human evolution, from the first stone tools until today, would not even get you halfway.
Now let's use a machine that actually left. Voyager 1 travels at about seventeen kilometers per second. That is sixty-one thousand kilometers an hour, about sixty-eight times faster than the jet.

If Voyager were pointed at Proxima, and it is not, it would arrive in about seventy-five thousand years. Written human history is about five thousand years old. You would need fifteen of them back to back.

Think about what that would mean for a crew. If one human generation is about twenty-five years, then about three thousand generations would be born, live and die on board before anyone arrived. Nobody who left would ever see the destination. Nobody who arrived would remember Earth.

On Christmas Eve, twenty twenty-four, NASA's Parker Solar Probe dove past the Sun at one hundred and ninety-two kilometers per second. Six hundred and ninety-two thousand kilometers an hour. New York to Tokyo in under a minute. Nothing humans have built has ever moved faster.

At that speed, Proxima is six thousand six hundred years away. That is longer than the pyramids have stood. And here is the catch. Parker only reaches that speed for a moment, while falling toward the Sun. We have no way to keep it going that fast.
If it could hold that speed, it would reach the Moon in about half an hour. Mars, at its closest, in a few days. And still, compared to the distance to the nearest star, it would barely have started.

chapter: Why we can't just go faster
text: Why not simply build something faster? Because speed is expensive. The energy of a moving object grows with the square of its speed. Go ten times faster, and you need one hundred times the energy. Go a thousand times faster, and you need a million times more.
That is the real wall between us and the stars. Not the distance. The energy.

Light, of course, does not care. It crosses the forty trillion kilometers in four point two four years. A child who waves goodbye to the launch would still be in primary school when the light arrives.

And even light is slow at this scale. If you sent a simple hello to Proxima, the earliest possible reply would reach you eight and a half years later. A conversation with our nearest neighbor would take most of a decade per sentence.

And what would be waiting there? In twenty sixteen, astronomers found a planet around Proxima. Proxima b is at least about as massive as Earth, and it circles its star every eleven point two days, inside the zone where liquid water could exist.

But Proxima is a red dwarf, and a flare star. It regularly blasts its planet with ultraviolet and X-ray radiation far stronger than anything Earth gets from the Sun. Whether anything could live there, nobody knows.

chapter: So how long would YOU need?
text: So, how long would you need? On foot: nine hundred and seventeen million years. By car: forty-six million. By jet: five million. Voyager: seventy-five thousand. Our fastest probe ever: six thousand six hundred. Light: four point two four years.
A human life is about eighty years. With anything we have ever built, you would not make it. Neither would your great-great-great-grandchildren.

The only serious plan on the table is called Breakthrough Starshot. Probes the size of a postage stamp, pushed by giant lasers to about a fifth of the speed of light. Each one would weigh about a gram. About twenty years to the Alpha Centauri system. It is a proposal. It is not built.
Next week: how far Voyager 1 has really gone, and what it will meet first. Which of these five would you have bet on? Tell me in the comments.
